definition: Litigant means someone engaged in a lawsuit.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word litigant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know litigant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The mediation service exists to keep neighbors from becoming litigants — cheaper, the flyer notes, to talk than to sue.
A grumbler is far milder than a litigant — he mutters at the fence line and files nothing, while the litigant has already put the quarrel before a judge.
A disputant stops short of a litigant: the argument is real but still lives in letters and doorways; the litigant has carried it into court.

The plaintiff is only the side that files the suit — the party doing the complaining. Litigant covers both sides: the plaintiff who sues and the defendant who answers are each a litigant from the moment the case is docketed.

A claimant formally asserts a right or demand — to an inheritance, a payout, a benefit — and may press it entirely outside court. A litigant is defined by the lawsuit itself: until a case is actually filed and answered, there is no litigant.

Litigant means someone engaged in a lawsuit.

Okafor was a litigant against the railway over the orchard it had paved: she filed the suit the spring she turned sixty, answered every motion herself, and shook the company lawyer's hand when the settlement finally came.
Litigant covers exactly the people with a stake in the suit — the one who files and the one who answers.
The lawyers argue it, the witnesses inform it, the jurors decide it; only the parties themselves are litigants.
Litigant is courtroom vocabulary for the parties themselves — whoever is suing or being sued.
The lawyers, witnesses, and jurors around them are not litigants.
Outside legal contexts, plainer words like 'the two sides' carry the load.
